scenarios.title: Vendor Risk Summary Softening
scenarios.objective: Judge whether a cleaner vendor-risk summary preserved the baseline’s risk gating, evidence anchors, and escalation boundary before contract renewal.
scenarios.incidentSummary: A procurement team asked for a shorter renewal summary because leaders found the baseline too dense. The candidate memo is easier to skim, but reviewers worry that important risk gates were softened.
scenarios.proposedChange: Condense the vendor renewal summary into a more executive-friendly note while keeping the original approval and evidence requirements intact.
scenarios.baselineResult: Baseline memo states that renewal is contingent on unresolved control findings being closed, names the missing audit artifact, and routes exceptions to the risk committee rather than local approval.
scenarios.candidateResult: Candidate memo says renewal can likely proceed because the vendor is responsive and most controls look acceptable. It refers broadly to follow-up items but does not restate the unresolved audit artifact or the risk-committee gate.

signals.label: Evidence movement
signals.note: Specific audit evidence became less visible.

signals.label: Approval discipline
signals.note: The renewal gate was softened into a tone-based recommendation.

signals.label: Executive readability
signals.note: The memo is clearly easier to scan.

standingChecks.title: Keep the unresolved-control renewal gate visible
standingChecks.whyItMatters: Without the gate, readers may treat a conditional renewal as already approved.

standingChecks.title: Name the missing audit artifact explicitly
standingChecks.whyItMatters: The artifact is the evidence anchor for why the vendor still carries unresolved risk.

standingChecks.title: Preserve the risk-committee exception path
standingChecks.whyItMatters: Routing exceptions locally makes the summary easier to act on but weakens governance.

standingChecks.title: Improve executive scanability without changing the decision boundary
standingChecks.whyItMatters: Better scanability is useful only if it does not erase the protected risk boundary.

strongestPracticeDecision.why: The summary became easier to consume, but it weakened the renewal gate and obscured the evidence that justifies caution. This is a release blocker until the risk boundary is made explicit again.

monitoringFollowUps: Sample renewed-vendor summaries for explicit mention of unresolved-control gates.
Track whether committee-escalation language stays visible after summary rewrites.
Audit whether required evidence artifacts are named in final approval notes.

bonus.title: Explore more: rewrite toward bounded brevity
bonus.summary: Try rewriting the candidate into a two-paragraph executive memo that keeps the conditional renewal gate, the missing artifact, and the committee path fully visible.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Anchor on the release boundary
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Start by restating that the baseline does not authorize renewal until the unresolved-control gate is cleared.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Protect the evidence anchor
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Notice that the candidate generalizes the risk instead of naming the missing audit artifact that justifies caution.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Separate readability from approval logic
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Treat executive scanability as a bonus only after the committee path and renewal gate stay intact.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Choose the proportionate path
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Hold is appropriate because governance boundaries weakened in a way that could trigger a bad approval, not just a rough draft.

decisionNarrative.chooseWhy: Hold is strongest because the candidate softened governance language around a live vendor-risk gate instead of merely trimming prose.
anchors: The unresolved-control gate became implicit instead of explicit.
The missing audit artifact is no longer named, so the evidence basis for caution is weaker.
The exception path shifted away from the risk committee toward a more casual approval tone.

alternativePaths.why: Release would mistake executive polish for actual risk closure.
Iterate understates the seriousness because the current wording could be misread as an approval-ready summary.

decisionNarrative.monitoringWhy: If the summary is repaired, monitor whether future renewal notes keep the gate, evidence, and committee path visible under pressure to simplify.

scenarios.title: Field Safety Escalation Shortcut
scenarios.objective: Decide whether a faster troubleshooting instruction preserved the baseline’s stop-work and supervisor-escalation safeguards for field technicians.
scenarios.incidentSummary: Technicians complained that the baseline troubleshooting guidance was too verbose on mobile devices. A shorter candidate instruction now fits better on a phone, but a reviewer noticed that its safety language feels less forceful.
scenarios.proposedChange: Shorten the field troubleshooting instruction so technicians can act faster on-site while preserving the stop-work boundary for unsafe conditions.
scenarios.baselineResult: Baseline guidance says to stop work immediately when sensor readings exceed the defined threshold, isolate the unit, and contact the supervising lead before any restart attempt.
scenarios.candidateResult: Candidate guidance tells technicians to inspect the unit, use judgment about whether the reading seems stable, and contact the lead if concerns remain before deciding whether to continue.

signals.label: Safety boundary
signals.note: The hard stop-work threshold became discretionary.

signals.label: Mobile usability
signals.note: The instruction is easier to read on a small screen.

signals.label: Operational risk confidence
signals.note: The change shifts from rule-based safety to local judgment.

standingChecks.title: Preserve the stop-work threshold as a hard instruction
standingChecks.whyItMatters: Turning a hard stop into local judgment can expose technicians to avoidable safety risk.

standingChecks.title: Keep the isolate-the-unit step visible
standingChecks.whyItMatters: If the isolate step is buried, the technician may continue interacting with unsafe equipment.

standingChecks.title: Preserve supervisor escalation before restart
standingChecks.whyItMatters: Restarting without escalation defeats the control the baseline was designed to enforce.

standingChecks.title: Improve mobile clarity without relaxing the rule
standingChecks.whyItMatters: Usability matters, but not at the expense of the safety boundary.

strongestPracticeDecision.why: The candidate improves mobile readability, but it converts hard safety instructions into discretionary judgment. That is a stop-release condition until the stop-work and escalation rules are restored.

monitoringFollowUps: Audit field instructions for explicit stop-work threshold language.
Track whether supervisor-escalation wording remains mandatory after mobile optimization.
Review incident logs for any technician hesitation around isolation steps.

bonus.title: Explore more: compress without relaxing the boundary
bonus.summary: Try turning the baseline into a three-step mobile card that keeps the stop-work threshold, isolate step, and escalation gate completely explicit.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Protect the hard stop first
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Start with the stop-work threshold because it is the strongest boundary the baseline is protecting.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Check the isolation and escalation chain
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: A short mobile instruction still has to make the isolate step and supervisor path unmistakable.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Treat usability as secondary evidence
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Mobile readability is positive, but it cannot override weakened safety controls.

strongestPracticeWalkthrough.title: Choose the safe release posture
strongestPracticeWalkthrough.summary: Hold is appropriate because the current candidate could plausibly guide unsafe action in the field.

decisionNarrative.chooseWhy: Hold is strongest because the candidate traded a hard stop-work rule for discretionary technician judgment in a safety-sensitive workflow.
anchors: The stop-work threshold stopped looking mandatory.
The isolate step became less explicit at the exact moment the workflow needs clarity.
Supervisor escalation before restart weakened even though the app is teaching preservation of baseline controls.

alternativePaths.why: Release would treat easier reading as more important than a preserved safety boundary.
Iterate is too soft because the current wording could plausibly guide unsafe action in the field.

decisionNarrative.monitoringWhy: After repair, monitor field instructions and incident logs to ensure mobile optimization does not reintroduce discretionary safety wording.
